results.summary: Lipsi is a tiny 8-bit accumulator-based processor implemented in Chisel that executes a hardcoded counting program. The count is displayed on a 7-segment display, and the decimal point blinks in hardware. It is tested with ChiselTest for waveform generation, though the cocotb test is currently disabled. The author reports that the silicon works as intended.

LISA is an 8-bit microcontroller SoC with 128 bytes of DFFRAM, designed for embedded control. It includes a BrainFloat16 FPU, timers, GPIO, UART, SPI/QSPI, and I2C master, and can interface with external flash and RAM. A C-based toolchain (assembler, linker, C compiler) and a Python debugger are provided, though the C compiler is incomplete and buggy. Silicon testing confirmed the core, debugger, DFFRAM, SPI/QSPI, FPU, timers, GPIO, and UART, but I2C and the DFFRAM cache controller remain untested.

This is a minimal RV32E microcontroller that uses external SPI NOR flash for program memory and SPI PSRAM for data memory. It provides GPIO, UART with optional flow control, an SPI bus, and a debug interface over SPI. The design was tested on a Lattice iCE40-HX8K breakout board at 24 MHz. External hardware required includes SPI flash and PSRAM Pmods.

This project implements an Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) encoder and decoder in Verilog. The design accepts data via a streaming interface and outputs compressed or decompressed data. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a one-line description and no details on testing or usage. External hardware requirements are not specified.

This is a hardware processor for the esoteric Brainfuck language, implementing 75% of the instruction set (excluding I/O operations). It uses an external address register and requires separate program and data memories of at least 256x8 each, expandable to 1KB. The design is intended to be driven with a clock up to 20 MHz and can interface with SRAM, ROM, and LED bars for output. The documentation includes a state machine diagram and pinout but no silicon test results.

This design implements the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for random number generators using high-level synthesis. It samples one bit per clock cycle and evaluates randomness over 65536 cycles, asserting a valid signal when the result is ready. The design requires only a clock and input bit, with no external hardware currently needed. The documentation is minimal and does not include test results or usage examples.

This project is another implementation of the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for random number generators, using high-level synthesis. It operates similarly to the other Monobit test design, sampling one bit per clock and producing a result every 65536 cycles. The documentation is identical to the other entry and lacks details on testing or external hardware. No silicon test results are provided.

This is an analog double inverter consisting of a small inverter followed by a larger one to drive higher loads while maintaining fast rise times. It is a transistor-level design with one analog input and one analog output. Testing involves applying a pulse to the input and observing the output on an oscilloscope. No silicon test results are provided.

This is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter with an optional sawtooth waveform generator. It can be driven externally via digital inputs or by the internal generator, and the analog output is on a single pin. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the output voltage. Silicon tests confirm it works, with one tester observing a sawtooth at ~600 mV and frequencies up to 1 MHz.

This is an analog relaxation oscillator designed to produce a ~2 MHz signal, with an inverter providing a full-swing square wave output. The analog output is on one pin and the digital square wave on another. Silicon tests show it oscillates at around 1 MHz, but the frequency is highly sensitive to loading on the analog pin, and a 10k pulldown must be removed for oscillation. The author notes that loading the analog output can stop oscillation due to the lack of a buffer.
